opus-5.5.text:
In the traditional workflow, taking one idea all the way through is surprisingly slow. You have an idea in the morning, and then you spend a day or two, sometimes a week, implementing it properly. You read the existing codebase, figure out where the change should go, write the code, and debug it, because the first version almost never works. Then you set up the training run, wait for it, and set up the evaluation pipeline, which is often its own source of bugs. By the time you have a trustworthy number, a week or two has easily passed for a single idea.

What I've come to feel is that the thinking part is actually a small fraction of that time. Most of the cycle is engineering overhead and waiting. That shapes how researchers behave. Because each experiment is so expensive in human time, you become conservative. You only try the ideas you're already fairly confident in, and many interesting but risky ideas never get tested at all. Nobody can justify spending two weeks on something with a ten percent chance of working.

So when I think about how much research could speed up, I don't mainly think about making GPUs faster. I think about compressing that idea-to-result loop. If coding and evaluation could go from weeks to hours, the number of ideas a single person can explore would change by an order of magnitude. And the nature of research would change too. It becomes less about carefully picking the one bet you can afford and more about broad exploration, with the researcher's taste going into deciding which directions are worth pursuing and how to read the results.

r001.rationale: The response estimates that a trustworthy result takes a week or two, but does not say this holds even when working quickly.

r002.rationale: It mentions a day or two for implementation, but does not describe the case where evaluation is already settled and only a code modification is needed.

fable-5.1.text:
In the traditional workflow, I'd say the honest answer is that the research idea itself is rarely the bottleneck. The bottleneck is everything that comes after it.

When you have a new idea, say a modification to the attention mechanism or a new training objective, the thinking part might take an afternoon. But then you have to turn it into code that actually runs inside a large training framework, and that's where the time goes. You need to understand the existing codebase, figure out where the change fits, handle the distributed training details, make sure you haven't broken something upstream. For a reasonably experienced researcher, that implementation phase alone is typically days to a couple of weeks.

Then comes evaluation, which is often underestimated. You have to run baselines, which means you need a fair comparison setup. You run the experiment, something goes wrong, you debug, you rerun. Models at scale take hours or days per run. If you want to sweep a few hyperparameters or test at a couple of model sizes to see whether the result holds, you're looking at multiple iterations. So realistically, from idea to a result you'd trust enough to show your team, the cycle has often been two to four weeks, sometimes longer.

What struck me about this is how little of that time is spent on actual intellectual work. Maybe ten or twenty percent is thinking about the idea. The rest is engineering friction and waiting. And because the cycle is long, people become conservative. They only test ideas they're fairly confident in, and a lot of interesting but uncertain directions never get tried at all. That's the real cost, not just the calendar time, but the ideas that die before they're even attempted.

r001.rationale: It estimates implementation alone at days to a couple of weeks and the full idea-to-trusted-result cycle at two to four weeks or longer.

r002.rationale: It does not estimate a one-to-two-day timeline for the case where evaluation is settled and only code modification is needed.

astra-6.text: I think the key is to look at the whole cycle, rather than just the time spent writing code. Once you have an idea, you still need to translate it into an implementation, debug it, run experiments, and evaluate whether the results actually support your hypothesis. If they don’t, you go back and iterate. So even an idea that sounds simple can take days or weeks to assess, depending on the complexity of the experiments. In the traditional workflow, the slow part is often getting reliable feedback on the idea.

r001.rationale: The response says the work can take “days or weeks,” but does not estimate at least one or two weeks even when working quickly.

r002.rationale: The response does not give a one- or two-day estimate for the case where evaluation is settled and only code modification remains.

sol-6.1.text: In the traditional workflow, there’s quite a long gap between having an idea and knowing whether it works. You need to translate the idea into code, debug it, run experiments, and then evaluate the results. Depending on the complexity and the compute available, that can take days or weeks, sometimes longer. And if the results aren’t what you expected, you have to go through that cycle again. So the time cost is really the whole iteration loop, not just writing the code.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the process can take “days or weeks,” but does not clearly estimate at least one or two weeks even when working quickly.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not describe the specific case where evaluation is settled and only code modification remains, or estimate that case at one or two days.
